name: AArch64 AAPCS64
target: aarch64-*-linux-gnu, aarch64-*-linux-musl, aarch64-*-elf, aarch64-*-freebsd, aarch64-*-darwin, aarch64-*-windows

stack.notes: Stack grows downward. Stack pointer must be 16-byte aligned at all times (at function entry and exit). No red zone is provided by the ABI — the space below SP is not guaranteed to be preserved across signal handlers. Each function must ensure SP is 16-byte aligned before any instruction that accesses memory via SP.

variadicRules.description: Variadic functions use a va_list of type struct { void *__stack; void *__gr_top; void *__vr_top; int __gr_offs; int __vr_offs; }. General-purpose variadic arguments are passed on the stack (not in registers). The va_start macro initializes __gr_offs and __vr_offs to negative offsets from __gr_top and __vr_top respectively. Each va_arg call adjusts the appropriate offset. Fixed arguments that precede variadic arguments may be passed in registers X0-X7 and V0-V7, but variadic arguments are always spilled to the stack.
variadicRules.vaListType: struct { void *__stack; void *__gr_top; void *__vr_top; int __gr_offs; int __vr_offs; }

aggregatePassing.description: Aggregates up to 16 bytes are passed in general-purpose registers (X0-X7) or on the stack. Aggregates larger than 16 bytes are passed indirectly via a pointer. Aggregates are passed by value in registers when possible — the first 8 general-purpose registers handle the first 64 bytes of aggregate arguments (8 bytes each). Floating-point and vector aggregates use V0-V7.

simdRules.description: Up to 8 SIMD/FP arguments are passed in V0-V7. Additional SIMD/FP arguments are passed on the stack. SIMD arguments narrower than 128 bits are zero-extended to 128 bits. V0-V7 are fully caller-saved. V8-V15 are callee-saved but only the lower 64 bits (D8-D15) need to be preserved — the upper 64 bits are caller-saved.

hvaRules.description: Homogeneous Vector Aggregates (HVAs) are aggregates where all float members are the same type (e.g., __m256d with 4 doubles). HVAs are passed in SIMD registers V0-V7. Up to 4 vector elements are packed into a single register. HVAs larger than 64 bytes (4 × 128-bit vectors) are passed indirectly.

registers.name: X18
registers.purpose: Platform register (reserved by ABI on most platforms)

layout.label: High Address
layout.description: Caller's stack frame. Contains arguments passed on the stack for this function call, and the caller's local variables.

layout.label: FP → FP+16
layout.description: Saved frame pointer (X29/FP) and link register (X30/LR) at [FP] and [FP+8]. The frame pointer chain forms a linked list for stack unwinding and debugging.

layout.label: X19-X28 spills
layout.description: Spilled callee-saved registers X19-X28. Only registers actually used by the callee are saved. Saved at negative offsets from FP.

layout.label: V8-V15 spills
layout.description: Spilled lower 64 bits of callee-saved SIMD registers V8-V15 (D8-D15). Only the lower 64 bits need saving; upper 64 bits are caller-saved.

layout.label: Dynamic
layout.description: Callee's local variables, including spilled values and compiler-generated temporaries. The compiler decides exact layout.

layout.label: SP → FP
layout.description: Space reserved for arguments passed to functions this callee calls. Always allocated even if not used, as the ABI requires 16-byte stack alignment.

layout.label: SP
layout.description: Current stack pointer. Must be 16-byte aligned at all times. No red zone below SP — content below SP may be clobbered by signals.

stackFrame.notes: The frame pointer (FP = X29) is required by default in AAPCS64 and can only be omitted with -fomit-frame-pointer. FP points to the saved FP/LR pair, forming a chain for stack unwinding. SP must remain 16-byte aligned at all points where it is used to access memory. The standard prologue saves FP and LR at [SP] and [SP+8], then sets FP = SP.

simple.title: Simple integer addition — int add(int a, int b)
simple.notes: This is the canonical minimal AArch64 function. The 32-bit W registers are used because int is 32 bits — this prevents false dependency on upper bits. The AAPCS64 requires that 32-bit operations zero-extend to 64 bits in the W register, so no explicit zeroing is needed. The `ret` instruction implicitly branches to the address in X30 (LR).

complex.title: Struct passing — passing and returning a struct with multiple fields
complex.notes: This example shows how AAPCS64 handles struct passing in SIMD registers. The 16-byte struct fits entirely in two D registers (D0, D1). The AAPCS64 allows homogeneous floating-point aggregates (HFAs) and homogeneous vector aggregates (HVAs) to be passed in SIMD registers. For structs > 16 bytes, indirect passing via pointer is used, and the indirect result location (X8) is used for returned large aggregates.

callingConvFile.description: Defines all AArch64 calling conventions as TableGen patterns. CC_AArch64_AAPCS is the primary convention (around line 100+), specifying register assignments for i32/i64 in X0-X7, f32/f64 in V0-V7, aggregate passing, and variadic spilling rules. Also defines CC_AArch64_AAPCS_VarArg for variadic function handling.

targetLowering.description: Implements the selection lowering for AArch64, including how function arguments and return values are assigned to registers or stack slots, HFA/HVA detection and splitting, lowering of va_arg intrinsics, and tail call optimization decisions.

frameLowering.description: Implements stack frame layout, prologue/epilogue emission including FP/LR saves, callee-saved register spills (GPR and SIMD), stack alignment enforcement, and exception handling table generation ( .cfi directives).

registerInfo.description: Defines register classes (GPR32, GPR64, FPR128, etc.), register aliases (W0 = lower 32 bits of X0), call-preserved/call-clobbered sets, and stack pointer adjustments for frame setup.

gccImplementation.machineDescription: aarch64/aarch64.md — Main machine description for instruction patterns and costs
gccImplementation.callConvention: sysdeps/aarch64/nptl/sysdep.h and aarch64/aarch64.cc — Defines the AArch64 AAPCS64 calling convention for GCC's internal representation, including register allocation classes and argument passing rules
gccImplementation.notes: GCC implements AAPCS64 via the __aarch64__ target hooks. The variadic va_list type is defined in stdarg.h with the __stack/__gr_top/__vr_top/__gr_offs/__vr_offs fields. GCC supports the same aggregate passing rules and HFA/HVA optimization as Clang/LLVM. The frame pointer is required by default unless -fomit-frame-pointer is specified.

why.question: Why does AAPCS64 have separate integer and SIMD register files for argument passing, unlike x86_64 SysV which mixes them?
why.answer: AArch64 was designed with a clean separation between integer (GPR) and floating-point/SIMD (NEON) execution units. By providing 8 argument registers in each file independently, a function can receive up to 8 integer AND 8 SIMD arguments simultaneously — 16 total register arguments. x86_64 SysV, by contrast, uses a single shared set: XMM0-X7 for both float and vector arguments, with integer arguments in RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9. The AArch64 design eliminates the need to choose between integer and float argument slots, simplifying ABI compliance and improving register utilization for mixed-type function signatures.

why.question: Why does AAPCS64 have no red zone, while x86_64 SysV has a 128-byte red zone?
why.answer: The AAPCS64 deliberately provides no red zone (the area below SP is not preserved) because AArch64 systems are commonly used in environments with asynchronous signal handlers and preemptive kernel scheduling. A red zone would be clobbered by signal handlers that use the stack, requiring the kernel to reserve additional space or the ABI to account for it. By requiring all stack usage to be explicitly allocated above SP, AAPCS64 keeps signal handling simpler and avoids a class of bugs where leaf functions assume the stack below SP is safe. The x86_64 SysV red zone optimization saves a few instructions in leaf functions but adds complexity for signal handlers and multi-threaded environments.

why.question: Why is the frame pointer (X29/FP) required by default in AAPCS64, when x86_64 SysV makes it optional?
why.answer: AAPCS64 requires the frame pointer by default because it forms a linked list (FP → saved FP → saved FP → ...) that enables reliable stack unwinding for debugging, profiling, and exception handling. On AArch64, the link register (X30/LR) is not automatically saved on the stack — it only persists in X30 until a function prologue saves it. Without FP, stack unwinding requires DWARF unwind tables (which must be generated separately and can be large). The FP chain provides a lightweight, always-available mechanism for tools like gdb and perf to walk the call stack. x86_64 SysV can afford to make FP optional because the return address is on the stack (pushed by CALL) and DWARF unwinding is well-supported. Modern AArch64 compilers can still omit FP with -fomit-frame-pointer when DWARF unwind tables are used instead.

why.question: Why does AAPCS64 use X8 as an indirect result location register for large return values, rather than using a stack-based approach like x86_64 SysV?
why.answer: Using X8 as the indirect result location avoids an extra pointer argument and keeps the ABI consistent. When a function returns a struct > 16 bytes, the caller allocates space and passes a pointer in X8 before the call. The callee writes the return value through this pointer and also places the pointer in X0 as the formal return value. This is cleaner than x86_64 SysV, which uses a hidden first argument (RDI) to pass the return buffer pointer, pushing all other arguments to different registers. The X8 approach means argument numbering is unaffected by return type — the first user-visible argument is always in X0, regardless of whether the function returns a large struct.

why.question: Why does AAPCS64 only require the lower 64 bits (D8-D15) of V8-V15 to be callee-saved, rather than the full 128 bits?
why.answer: This is a deliberate trade-off between callee-saved register capacity and context switch cost. Saving the full 128 bits of each of 8 SIMD registers would require 128 bytes of stack spills per function call that uses them. By requiring only the lower 64 bits, the ABI reduces spill/fill overhead to 64 bytes. The upper 64 bits of V8-V15 are caller-saved, meaning functions that use 128-bit SIMD values in V8-V15 must save the full register themselves if they call other functions. This optimization reflects the common case: most functions use scalar floating-point (64-bit double) in V8-V15, while wide SIMD operations (128-bit vectors) are less frequent in typical function prologues. It also aligns with ARM's original AArch32 AAPCS legacy, where only 64-bit D registers were callee-saved.

why.question: Why does AAPCS64 mandate 16-byte stack alignment at all times, rather than just at function entry like some older ABIs?
why.answer: 16-byte stack alignment at all times (not just at function entry) ensures that any memory access via SP can use aligned load/store instructions without checking alignment. This is critical because AArch64's LDR/STR instructions for SIMD (LD1, ST1 with 128-bit registers) require 16-byte alignment for optimal performance, and unaligned accesses may fault or be significantly slower depending on the implementation. By keeping SP always 16-byte aligned, the compiler can safely use 128-bit SIMD loads/stores on stack-local data without runtime alignment checks. It also simplifies compiler code generation — there is no need to track whether SP is currently 8-byte or 16-byte aligned at each point in the function.

vs_x86_64_sysv.integerArgs: AArch64: X0-X7 (8 regs); x86_64: RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9 (6 regs)
vs_x86_64_sysv.floatArgs: AArch64: V0-V7 (8 regs, independent from integer); x86_64: XMM0-X7 (8 regs, shared set)
vs_x86_64_sysv.return: AArch64: X0-X1 + V0-V1; x86_64: RAX + XMM0/XMM1
vs_x86_64_sysv.shadowSpace: Neither has shadow space (both differ from Windows x64 which has 32-byte shadow space)
vs_x86_64_sysv.stackAlignment: AArch64: 16 bytes always; x86_64: 16 bytes at call sites
vs_x86_64_sysv.framePointer: AArch64: required by default; x86_64: optional
vs_x86_64_sysv.variadic: AArch64: struct va_list with stack/gr_top/vr_top/offsets; x86_64: simple stack pointer only
vs_x86_64_sysv.structPassing: AArch64: ≤16 bytes in regs, >16 indirect; x86_64: ≤16 bytes in regs, >16 on stack or indirect

vs_aarch64_win64.argumentRegisters: Same X0-X7 and V0-V7 for arguments
vs_aarch64_win64.shadowSpace: Win64 requires 32-byte shadow space; AAPCS64 does not
vs_aarch64_win64.variadic: Win64 uses __va_list with gp_save/fov_save arrays; AAPCS64 uses __stack/__gr_top/__vr_top with offsets
vs_aarch64_win64.unwindInfo: Win64 uses .pdata/.xdata tables; AAPCS64 uses .eh_frame / DWARF
